name: Quit smoking / vaping

lead: Quitting tobacco or vaping is cited as a way to avoid or reduce 'smoker's face', the pattern of wrinkles, sagging and a dull yellowish or grayish complexion seen in many long-term smokers.

Medical sources attribute these changes to reduced oxygen and nutrient supply to skin, narrowed blood vessels, oxidative stress and breakdown of collagen and elastin. The link between smoking and facial aging is documented in observational research. No trials of quitting for appearance were found, and vaping and facial aging have not been studied.

paras: People quit through whatever route works for them, including nicotine replacement, medication or support programmes, and often mention it as part of a broader skin and anti-aging routine. Skin blood flow is the step through which any appearance change is expected.
Quitting itself carries no appearance-specific risks in the sources reviewed. Smoking is linked to many serious diseases, so quitting has health benefits well beyond looks.

web.title: What happens to your skin when you quit smoking - Healthline

chain: Better skin blood flow and collagen
angle.text: Quitting tobacco or vaping is cited to avoid or reduce smoker's face, with its wrinkles, sagging and dull yellowish complexion. Less tobacco and nicotine exposure means better skin blood flow and collagen, and a brighter, less wrinkled complexion. The link between smoking and facial aging comes from observational research.

lead: Quitting smoking or vaping is discussed in skincare and looksmaxxing circles as a way to protect and improve the skin, teeth and overall look of the face. Long-term smokers often show a recognisable set of facial changes called 'smoker's face': wrinkling, sagging, a greyish or yellowish complexion and staining of the teeth and mouth [1]. Stopping tobacco is the step people take to stop adding to that pattern, and some report a clearer, more even complexion afterwards [2].

The skin-related reasons given include better oxygen and nutrient supply to the skin, less breakdown of collagen and elastin, and less oxidative stress [1][2]. A 1985 BMJ paper by D. Model, cited on Wikipedia, found the characteristic features in about 46% of continuing smokers but about 8% of former smokers with a similar smoking history [1]. A health-information article summarising several small studies reports less redness, tobacco staining and discolouration after quitting, and renewed collagen production in a small 2019 study [2].

Vaping is a related but separate topic. E-cigarettes avoid combustion, and a 2025 Cochrane review cited on Wikipedia found nicotine e-cigarettes more effective than nicotine replacement therapy for quitting smoking [3]. Researchers studying vaping have mostly looked at lung and cardiovascular effects rather than the skin [4][5][6]. On looksmax.org some users describe nicotine as an appetite suppressant for getting lean, while others say they quit because of concerns about growth and health [7][8][9].

This article covers both halves of the topic: what is documented about stopping cigarettes for appearance, and how vaping and nicotine come up in appearance-focused communities, including the withdrawal experience that people describe when they stop.

paras: Smoker's face refers to the facial changes seen in many long-term tobacco smokers, including wrinkling, sagging, a grey tone to the skin, hair loss and mouth changes such as staining, gum disease and bad breath [1]. Wikipedia classes this as extrinsic ageing, meaning ageing driven by an external exposure rather than by time alone [1]. Quitting removes the ongoing exposure behind these features.

Health-information summaries describe improvements after quitting. One review is said to show age spots and discolouration beginning to fade within about a month; a small 2013 study (Ishiwata and colleagues) reported significantly less redness and tobacco staining, with skin colour changes starting to reverse four to twelve weeks after stopping; and a small 2010 study (Serri and colleagues, titled 'Quitting smoking rejuvenates the skin') estimated a 'biological age' reduction of 13 years based on brightness, smoothness, elasticity and colouring [2]. The same summary notes that more research is needed on how quitting affects existing wrinkles and that timing varies between people [2].

Writers who discuss quitting for looks often pair it with other routine skin habits. The Healthline summary lists balanced diet, regular cardio, sleep, daily sunscreen, a basic cleanse-and-moisturise routine, and products such as vitamin C serums, niacinamide and retinol as complementary steps, along with in-office treatments such as microneedling, fillers and laser resurfacing [2].

Proposed mechanisms include higher levels of enzymes (matrix metalloproteinases) that break down collagen, elastin and proteoglycans, lower antioxidant levels such as vitamin C, narrowing of facial blood vessels by tobacco chemicals, a build-up of free radicals causing oxidative stress, and reduced levels of the enzymes glutathione peroxidase and glutathione reductase that help protect tissue [1]. The Healthline summary adds that tobacco smoke is linked to pigmentation that can make skin look grey, reddish or sallow, and that smoking can worsen conditions such as psoriasis and eczema [2]. Quitting is described as allowing collagen production to resume, based on a small 2019 study [2]; the summary's own reference list names a paper on collagen-induced platelet activation, so the study's focus is not purely cosmetic [2].

Wikipedia lists staining or yellowing of teeth, gum disease, tooth decay, tooth loss, dry socket, reduced sense of taste and halitosis among smoker's face features [1]. Reduced odour and fewer stains are among the reasons users give for choosing e-cigarettes over cigarettes [3].
Hair loss is listed alongside the facial features of smoker's face on Wikipedia [1].

The idea that smoking leaves a visible mark on the face was set out in the clinical literature in 1985, when D. Model published 'Smoker's face: an underrated clinical sign?' in the BMJ (21 December 1985) [1]. Jane E. Brody wrote about the topic for the New York Times on 19 June 1996, and public-health bodies including the UK Department of Health ('Smoker's Face: Beauty is only skin deep') and Action on Smoking and Health have used appearance as a theme in anti-smoking material [1].

Skin-specific quitting studies appeared in the 2010s, including the small studies of skin colour and skin 'biological age' summarised above [2]. Appearance messages have since become one of several approaches used in cessation campaigns aimed at young people, a group in which vaping is now more common than cigarette smoking [3].

Vaping devices heat a liquid, usually containing propylene glycol, glycerin, flavourings and often nicotine, and breathe the aerosol in. Heating produces by-products including formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein [3]. Wikipedia describes vaping as less harmful than smoking but not free of risk [3]. Reviews note that nicotine delivery through vaping has grown fast among young people and non-smokers, in addition to its use by people trying to leave cigarettes [4][10].

Research on vaping has concentrated on lung injury and on cardiovascular effects [4][5][11][6][12]. An American Heart Association scientific statement discusses patterns of use and potential cardiopulmonary harms [6]. Studies of vaping with facial appearance as the outcome were not located.

Early precursors include a 1927 patent for an electric vaporizer for medicinal compounds and Herbert Gilbert's 1963 patent for a smokeless, nicotine-free cigarette, neither of which was marketed [3]. The modern design is credited to Hon Lik, a Chinese pharmacist born in 1951 who started smoking at 18; he filed a priority application in 2003, and the first device, Ruyan, was manufactured in Shenyang in 2004 [13]. His original aim was to help himself quit smoking [13]. His company's e-cigarette business was sold to Imperial Brands in 2013 for $75 million [3].

JUUL launched in June 2015 and held over 72% of the monitored US market by August 2018 [3]. In 2022 the FDA denied JUUL's application to keep its products on the market, and in April 2023 the company agreed to pay $462 million to settle claims from six states and the District of Columbia over marketing to minors [3]. US youth e-cigarette use peaked in 2019 and had fallen substantially by 2024, when 7.8% of high-school students reported use; among youth users in 2024, 26.3% reported daily use and 87.6% used flavoured products [3].

A 2019 US outbreak of vaping-associated lung injury (EVALI) drew national attention to vaping safety. As of 4 February 2020, 2,758 cases had been reported across the country; the median age was 24 and about 86% of patients with substance-use data reported THC-containing products [14]. US health agencies identified vitamin E acetate, used as a thickener in illicit THC cartridges, as a strong culprit, detected in 29 of 29 lung biopsies examined by the CDC [14]. Review articles describe the clinical and pathological features of vaping-related lung injury [15].

Wikipedia's nicotine article states that nicotine reduces hunger and food intake and raises energy expenditure, and that most research finds it lowers body weight [16]. This is the basis of the appetite-suppression discussion in looksmaxxing forums, where some users describe vaping as a way to eat less during a cut [7][8].

The same article describes nicotine as highly addictive, with dependence able to develop within days. Withdrawal can bring anxiety, irritability, craving, low mood and trouble with sleep, memory and attention; symptoms peak within one to three days and can last several weeks [16]. Forum users describe the early days without nicotine in similar terms, and one T Nation poster noted that stopping brings 'severe psychological cravings' alongside insomnia and irritability [17][18]. Another T Nation member described swapping cigarettes for a vape and finding it harder to stop, alternating between gum, patches and the vape [19].

Randomised trials have tested programs for quitting vaping, including a text-message program for young adults (JAMA Internal Medicine, 2021), a text-message program for adolescents (JAMA, 2024) and a varenicline trial in youth (JAMA, 2025) [20][21][22]. Their outcomes concern quitting rates, not appearance. A 2025 Cochrane review cited on Wikipedia found nicotine e-cigarettes more effective than nicotine replacement therapy for smoking cessation, while noting that they have been tested less rigorously than replacement products [3]. A 2018 Cochrane review confirmed that nicotine replacement therapy increases quit success [16].

The US FDA has regulated e-cigarettes as tobacco products since 2016, requires photo ID for purchase and bans sales to minors; a 2022 law extended its authority to nicotine from any source, including synthetic nicotine [3]. The EU Tobacco Products Directive took effect in May 2016, limiting advertising, nicotine levels and flavours and setting an 18+ purchase age [3]. Japan bans nicotine e-cigarettes, as do Brazil, Singapore, Uruguay and India, and Australia restricted legal sales from 1 July 2024; critics of such restrictions argue they could expand illicit markets [3].

Posts on looksmax.org about nicotine are mixed. Some users describe vaping as an appetite suppressant that helped them lose weight and show a leaner face ('here comes the hollow cheeks'), with sweet-flavoured vapes helping candy cravings; replies from other users raise concerns about lungs and about growth in younger users [7][8][9]. Other threads describe the difficulty of the first days without nicotine [17]. Another thread asks directly whether vaping stunts height growth and development [23]. On T Nation, members discuss quitting vaping as part of structured training challenges [19].

No randomised trial of quitting smoking or vaping with facial appearance as the primary outcome was found. The skin findings come from observational work, such as the 1985 BMJ paper, and small studies summarised above [1][2]. Randomised trials of cessation programs measure whether people stop using nicotine [20][21][22]. Reviews of vaping examine lung and cardiovascular outcomes [4][5][12].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, vaping and nicotine come up both as a way to suppress appetite and get lean and as something users say they are trying to give up. Quitting for skin is discussed in skincare circles more than in forums. [7][8][9][17]
